newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Review of New Zealand CPI underway.
newsitem.headline: Review of New Zealand CPI underway.

text.p: Statistics New Zealand is laying the ground for a five-yearly review of the consumers' price index, a process which almost certainly will result in debate about the index's influence on monetary policy, the New Zealand Press Association reported on Tuesday.

Deputy government statistician Ian Ewing said the composition of an advisory committee, including international experts in the composition of consumer price indexes, was currently under discussion with Statistics Minister Maurice Williamson.
Once established, the committee would complete consideration of papers and conceptual issues before rebalancing of the CPI got under way in the second half of next year.
Ewing told NZPA uses of the CPI had changed over the years, and representation on the committee would reflect those changes.

While employer and union groups had been major users in the past, that had dwindled with the demise of centralised wage fixing after 1984, and the Treasury and Reserve Bank interests would be present on the committee given the importance of the CPI in monetary policy.

represent producers, consumers, employers and employee groups, major government policy agencies, in particular the Reserve Bank and Treasury, and possibly other groups within the community who may be affected by government policy as it affects prices," Ewing said.
"Papers are presented to the committee for advice and guidance and, as a result of that, we carry out a five-year rebase of the CPI, and the extent of that is governed in part by the committee."
Ewing said rebalancing of the CPI would involve considerations such as changes in spending behaviour in the last five years.

Households, for instance, have been spending less on clothing due to the impact of deregulation of the industry reducing prices, while imports of used Japanese cars have reduced transport costs and, thus, overall spending.
Statistics New Zealand's household economic survey had also found that people were spending less of their income on housing, Ewing said.
However, the treatment of housing is likely to come in for some solid debate with the Reserve Bank seen as arguing to have interest rates removed from any measure of its cost.
Ewing said there were opposing schools of thought on whether house ownership should be treated as an item of shelter or as an investment.
If it was accepted that housing was a consumption rather than an investment good, then there were issues of how housing was priced.
"Do you assume the cost is what you would get if you rented the house out, as against the actual costs of owning the house -- interest paid on mortgages, that sort of thing," Ewing said.

But even if elements of the CPI were removed for monetary policy purposes, a broader-based index could be more appropriate than one confined to measuring the impact of inflation on households, he said.
However, another index for monetary policy purposes would do little to allay Reserve Bank concerns about the CPI's impact in setting inflationary expectations, he suggested.
"The CPI has been the most prominent, well-known measure of inflation... even though it may have some technical limitations as a tool for measuring inflation," Ewing said.
